title: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodic seasons of extreme cold or drought are the most effective of all checks on increase.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodical seasons of extreme cold or drought, I believe to be the most effective of all checks.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “Effects of climate”. Scope: animal and plant populations, e.g. birds in severe winters

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Abundance and climate archives enable broad event studies, but ranking climate as the most effective of all checks requires consistently measured rivals that are usually absent. The climate effect is more resolvable than the superlative.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Link population growth and crash events to standardized cold and drought extremes, then compare their effect sizes with predation, disease, competition and ordinary resource limitation. Extremes having the largest recurrent effects supports the superlative claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Extreme events and biological responses are spatially mismatched.

Biotic checks are measured less consistently than weather.

fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.78
data adequacy: 0.58
discriminating power: 0.57
analysis feasibility: 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Population indices and climate layers can test whether bad years track cold and drought for well-monitored species. They cannot, by themselves, rank climate against predation, disease, and competition. The superlative is only partly approachable with long-term sites where causes were recorded, and that subset is small.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Attribute interannual changes in abundance to extreme cold or drought versus predation, disease, food, and competition, using a common mortality or growth currency. Climate extremes would be the most effective check if their standardized effects exceeded the others across species; comparable or larger biotic effects would refute the superlative.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Extremes are confounded with food shortage and predator success in the same season.

Most abundance series lack a cause-of-death field, so climate correlations are not a comparison among all checks.

'Most effective of all checks' needs a shared unit that different studies do not use.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.45
data existence: 0.58
discriminating power: 0.4
operationalizability: 0.56
